raw_text: {"schema_version":"chat_response_v1","response_type":"answer","answer_text":"AUG has two roles in translation, while the stop codons UAA, UAG and UGA only terminate synthesis. AUG serves as the start codon that initiates translation and also specifies methionine [ev_009]. An in-frame AUG encountered during elongation is read by a regular Met-tRNA, which inserts a non-formylated methionine [ev_004]. The three stop codons are UAA, UAG and UGA [ev_002], and they terminate protein synthesis and release the polypeptide from the translation machinery [ev_009]. When a stop codon reaches the A site, entry of a release factor terminates translation and the components dissociate [ev_006]. Release factors are recognized by the stop codon upon aligning with the A site, and they resemble tRNAs [ev_001]. Instead of adding an amino acid, the release factor instructs peptidyl transferase to add a water molecule to the carboxyl end of the P-site amino acid [ev_001]. This reaction forces the P-site amino acid to detach from its tRNA, so the newly made protein is released [ev_001]. The small and large ribosomal subunits then dissociate from the mRNA and from each other [ev_001], and the release factor binds and dissociates the components and frees the new protein [ev_007]. After many ribosomes have completed translation, the mRNA is degraded so its nucleotides can be reused [ev_001].","short_answer":null,"citations":["ev_009","ev_004","ev_002","ev_006","ev_001","ev_007"],"refusal_reason":null,"follow_up_questions":[],"confidence":0.8,"tutor_question":null,"learner_attempt_evaluation":null}
